title: Kaaba Overview
description: The Kaaba is a near-cubic stone building at the centre of the Grand Mosque in Mecca, and it is the holiest site in Islam and the direction of prayer for Muslims worldwide. Published dimensions are about 12.86 metres long, 11.03 metres wide, and 13.1 metres high, built of stone with marble and limestone, at published coordinates 21.4225 degrees north and 39.82617 degrees east. Its exterior is draped in the Kiswah, a black covering replaced annually, and its gilded door stands above ground level on one side. Pilgrims circle the building seven times counterclockwise in tawaf, walking in the Mataf around it, and the building's role as qibla means that prayer direction everywhere is measured toward this point. The origin and early rebuilding of the Kaaba are reported in Islamic tradition, and this pair keeps those accounts in their own labeled records, so that measured facts and tradition accounts are never blended in one sentence. This pair contains no image of any person and no depiction of any kind beyond words about a building.

title: Dimensions and Structure
description: Published dimensions for the Kaaba are 12.86 metres in length, 11.03 metres in width, and 13.1 metres in maximum height, and every figure in this record should be read as approximate, because sources vary slightly in how they measure a building that has been rebuilt, repaired, and re-clad over centuries. From those published figures the footprint is about 141.8 square metres, the perimeter is about 47.8 metres, the wall area is about 626 square metres, and the bounding volume is about 1,858 cubic metres, and the demo in this record computes exactly those derived figures so a reader can check them. The structure is essentially solid masonry with a small interior room, three wooden pillars reported in published summaries, a marble floor, and hanging lamps, and it is opened only rarely. The walls are not perfectly vertical in every survey, and the height is given as a maximum, which is why this record says maximum height rather than a single exact height. Where a later survey gives a different tenth of a metre, that difference is a measurement difference, not a different building.

title: Kiswah (Covering)
description: The Kiswah is the black cloth covering draped over the Kaaba, made of silk with a gold-embroidered band carrying calligraphy around the upper walls, and it is replaced annually in a published ceremony. A Kiswah factory was established in Mecca in 1928 according to published expansion history, so that the covering could be made locally rather than brought from elsewhere. The covering is fitted in panels around the four walls, with a separate section for the door, and its black colour against the white marble of the Mataf makes the Kaaba visible from every part of the mosque. The annual replacement is a fact about practice and manufacture, and the calligraphy on the band is described in published summaries in general terms only, because this record does not reproduce sacred text. The demo in this record estimates wall covering area from the published perimeter and height, before seams and openings, and that estimate is labeled as a model, not as a factory measurement.

title: Black Stone
description: The Black Stone, Hajar al-Aswad, is set in the eastern corner of the Kaaba in a silver frame, and it marks the starting point for tawaf, the circling of the Kaaba. What a visitor sees today is a set of dark fragments held in that frame, because published history reports that the stone was broken and its fragments rejoined with a silver ligament, and that it was removed from Mecca for a period in the 10th century CE after a raid, returning later. Those historical events are reported in published histories and are stated here as published history. The origin of the stone, and its meaning for pilgrims, are reported in Islamic tradition, and this record labels those accounts as tradition: traditions differ in detail about the stone's origin, and this record says that traditions differ rather than settling the difference. No physical description beyond the published setting is offered here, and no claim is made about the stone's composition beyond what published summaries state, because composition claims without a cited survey would be speculation.

title: Hijr Ismail
description: Hijr Ismail, also called the Hatim, is the semi-circular low wall on the north-west side of the Kaaba, enclosing an area that tradition associates with Ismail. That association is labeled tradition, and the wall's shape and place are stated as published facts: a low semi-circular marble wall standing apart from the Kaaba's walls, enclosing ground that pilgrims treat as part of the sanctuary circuit. In practice, pilgrims circling the Kaaba pass outside the wall, so that the enclosed area is included in the circuit, and that practice is a fact about tawaf as performed. The wall has been rebuilt and re-clad in the same modern works that reshaped the Mataf, and its present marble form belongs to those works. This record keeps the tradition association and the physical description in separate sentences, so that a reader can see which kind of statement each sentence is.

The roof is flat and carries a water spout on one side, and access to the roof is by an internal stair reported in published summaries. The interior is a small room with a marble floor, three wooden pillars, and hanging lamps according to published summaries, and it is opened only rarely for dignitaries and ceremonial occasions. This record deliberately keeps interior description at that general published level, because a fuller interior inventory is not in the public record used here, and inventing one would break the labeling rule. The door's height above ground is itself a practical fact: the building is entered, not walked into at ground level, and that shapes how opening ceremonies are staged.

title: Construction and Repairs Through History
description: The present Kaaba was built after the original building was damaged by fire during the siege of Mecca in 683 CE, according to published histories, and it has been repaired and rebuilt in stages ever since. The most disruptive single episode in published history is the Qarmatian raid of 930 CE, when the Black Stone was carried away, returning in 952 CE after a ransom arrangement reported in published histories. Later centuries brought Ottoman repairs and re-cladding, and Saudi-era works reshaped the surroundings, moved the Maqam Ibrahim enclosure for circling room, and renewed the Kiswah system with a local factory from 1928. The building's dimensions have therefore been measured at different times with slightly different results, which is why this pair labels all dimensions approximate. The origin of the first building is reported in Islamic tradition, and that account is labeled tradition wherever it appears in this pair, never blended with the dated repair sequence given here.

Later centuries brought Ottoman repairs and re-cladding, and Saudi-era works reshaped the surroundings, moved the Maqam Ibrahim enclosure for circling room, and renewed the Kiswah system with a local factory from 1928. The building's dimensions have therefore been measured at different times with slightly different results, which is why this pair labels all dimensions approximate. The origin of the first building is reported in Islamic tradition, and that account is labeled tradition wherever it appears in this pair, never blended with the dated repair sequence given here.

title: Materials
description: The published materials of the Kaaba are stone for the main masonry, marble and limestone in floors and facings, silk for the Kiswah with gold embroidery on its band, gilded metal for the door, and silver for the frame holding the Black Stone fragments. Each material has a visible job: stone carries the structure, marble gives a hard washable floor and facing, silk gives a covering that can be replaced annually, gilding marks the door, and silver holds fragments together in a single frame. Modern repairs have added modern mortars, metals, and fixings, but published summaries do not give a complete modern materials inventory, and this record does not invent one. Where a material is reported in tradition rather than in a survey, such as accounts of the stone's origin, this record labels it tradition. The materials list here is therefore a published summary, not a laboratory report, and it says so.

title: Misconceptions Corrected
